summary: This RFC extends the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation algorithm with Explicit Address Mappings, letting an operator define exact IPv6-to-IPv4 address pairs. This makes translation possible between arbitrary IPv6 endpoints that do not use the translation prefix and IPv4. It formally updates RFC 6145.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7757 adds an explicit mapping table to the stateless IPv4/IPv6 translation algorithm. Operators can pair IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes directly, while unmapped addresses continue to use the existing translation rule.

questions: what is an explicit address mapping table
how does eam differ from rfc 6052 translation
what is hairpinning in ip translation
subtitle: Translate selected IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes using an operator-configured table.

tldr.problem: Stateless IP/ICMP translation normally requires IPv6 addresses to follow a particular format containing an IPv4 address.
tldr.mechanism: An Explicit Address Mapping table pairs IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes. The translator finds the longest matching prefix and copies the remaining address bits between the two forms.
tldr.outcome: Operators can translate arbitrary IPv6 prefixes to IPv4 without replacing the standard algorithm for addresses that have no explicit mapping.

today: RFC 7757 is an Internet Standard. It updates RFC 6145 by adding explicit address mappings to the stateless translation algorithm.

sections.title: Why Explicit Address Mappings Are Needed
sections.content:
RFC 6145 translates IPv4 and IPv6 addresses using the format in RFC 6052. That requires an IPv6 node to use an IPv4-translatable IPv6 address, which may be scarce, incompatible with the network's address plan, or difficult to route and operate.

RFC 7757 adds a table-based alternative so an operator can map ordinary IPv6 addresses or prefixes to IPv4 prefixes without assigning a second IPv6 address to each node.
sections.plainLanguage: Some IPv6 networks cannot use addresses that embed IPv4 addresses. An explicit table lets an operator map the network's existing IPv6 addresses instead.

sections.title: The Explicit Address Mapping Table
sections.content:
An Explicit Address Mapping Table (EAMT) contains entries pairing an IPv4 prefix with an IPv6 prefix. If a prefix length is omitted, the implementation treats it as a single address: 32 bits for IPv4 and 128 bits for IPv6.

The IPv4 prefix must have no more suffix bits than its paired IPv6 prefix. When several entries match an address, the translator uses the entry with the longest common prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Each table row pairs one IPv4 network range with one IPv6 network range. When ranges overlap, the most specific matching row is used.

sections.title: Translating Addresses in Either Direction
sections.content:
For IPv4-to-IPv6 translation, the translator removes the matching IPv4 prefix, keeps the remaining address bits, and adds the paired IPv6 prefix. It pads the result with trailing zero bits if needed to reach 128 bits.

For IPv6-to-IPv4 translation, it removes the matching IPv6 prefix and adds the paired IPv4 prefix. If the result is longer than 32 bits, trailing bits are discarded. If no EAM matches, the translator uses the algorithm in RFC 6145 and its updates.
sections.plainLanguage: The translator replaces the matched prefix and carries the remaining address bits across. An address without a table match uses the existing SIIT translation algorithm.

sections.title: Handling IPv6 Traffic That Loops Back
sections.content:
Two IPv6 nodes covered by EAMs may communicate through the translator by using IPv4-converted IPv6 addresses. The translator may need to send the packet through translation twice so the reply follows a matching path back.

The RFC describes two approaches: simple hairpinning rules that avoid selected EAM translations, or intrinsic hairpinning that translates a packet back to IPv6 before forwarding it to the IPv4 network.
sections.plainLanguage: Two mapped IPv6 nodes may need the translator to loop traffic back into IPv6. The RFC gives two ways to keep the forward and return packets compatible.

sections.title: Overlapping Mappings and Checksums
sections.content:
Overlapping or identical prefixes in the table can make forward and reverse translations asymmetric. In some configurations, a packet translated in one direction will not return to its original address, so implementations may warn about overlapping entries or reject identical prefixes.

An EAM translation is not guaranteed to preserve a packet's checksum. The translator must account for checksum changes as part of the applicable SIIT processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Overlapping table entries can send a reply to a different address than the original sender. Operators should also know that mapped addresses do not guarantee a checksum-neutral translation.
